original_summary: An open ascending (English) auction for one object. Bidders with private valuations take turns raising the standing bid by at least a fixed increment or dropping out, and the last bidder left pays their bid and earns valuation minus price.

review.evidence: Bidding up to your own valuation and no further is a dominant strategy. The player dealt the highest valuation wins against any sensible opponent. 'Always pass' scores 0, which ties every other loser.
With one object and the dominant strategy known, the outcome is fixed by who was dealt the highest value. A skilled player cannot beat a worse player who holds a higher valuation.
The game is solved: bid to value. A strong player has nothing to improve on.
Valuations are hidden, but the dominant strategy needs no inference about them. Inference matters only for the price paid, not for who wins.
The payoff is valuation minus price, which is pure arithmetic.
It is text and turn-based, but turn-by-turn bidding runs for an unbounded number of steps. It is also a single one-shot event, not a round structure.

problems: P1: Bidding up to your valuation is dominant, so the auction is solved and takes no thought.
P2: Lottery trap: the player dealt the highest valuation wins, and good play cannot overcome a bad deal.
P3: A single object gives no planning over several rounds and no learning about opponents.
P4: Open-ended rotating bidding has no bound on steps and does not fit the platform's fixed per-round step limits.
P5: Under the winner rule, losing and passing are equivalent (both 0), so nothing distinguishes a cautious play from a passive one.

changes.what: Play 8 auctions in a row. Each player has one fixed budget of 40 coins for the whole game; unspent coins have no value except as a tiebreak.
changes.why: Truthful bidding now exhausts the budget on low-margin items. A player must plan which auctions to contest and save coins for later, so bidding to value stops being dominant.

changes.what: Every player owns an identical private deck of 8 valuations {2,4,6,8,10,12,14,16}, shuffled separately. One card is revealed privately to each player per round, so every value is used exactly once.
changes.why: All players receive the same total opportunity over the game. Luck changes only timing, which budgeting and reading opponents can correct for.

changes.what: Only the winner's valuation is revealed after each auction; drop-outs and bids are public.
changes.why: Players can count which values an opponent has already used and infer their remaining cards and budget from how they bid. This builds inference and opponent modelling across rounds.

changes.what: Each auction has at most 3 bidding steps. In each step, all active non-leaders at once either raise (a whole number at least 2 above the standing bid) or drop for good. Ties are broken by lower score, then by a rotating seat order.
changes.why: This keeps the ascending, open, drop-out character of an English auction. It is bounded and fits the step limits, and the cap on steps makes jump bids a meaningful signal.

changes.what: There are 3 to 5 players, and the highest total profit wins. Tie on profit goes to more coins left, then a draw. Overpaying can drive profit below zero.
changes.why: With three or more players the game is not zero-sum between any two. 'Always pass' scores 0 and loses to anyone who makes profitable purchases, and 'always bid high' goes negative.

changes.what: Add one simultaneous message per player before bidding each round.
changes.why: This allows non-binding bidding rings ('you take this one, I take the next'), bluffs about one's card and tests of trust. Only one player can win, so following a proposal can cost you.

keeps: An open ascending auction in which the standing bid and the provisional winner are public.
A minimum increment of 2 and drop-outs that are permanent for the item.
Private valuations, and a payoff to the winner of valuation minus price, with everyone else earning 0 on that item.

recommendation.reason: The ascending auction is a strong core. A budget across several auctions, balanced value decks and bounded simultaneous raise steps turn it into a planning and inference game inside the limits.

variation.name: Budget English Auctions
variation.summary: Players run 8 bounded open ascending auctions on a single 40-coin budget. Each player privately holds the same set of valuations in a different order, and the highest total profit wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP
1. Each player starts with 40 coins and a score of 0. Coins and scores are public.
2. Each player gets a private deck of 8 value cards: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Each deck is shuffled separately, and its order is secret.
3. Seats are numbered 1 to n.

EACH ROUND (8 rounds; round r):
1. Deal: every player privately sees the next card of their own deck. That is their value for this round's item.
2. Talk: every player writes one short message at the same time without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding.
3. Bidding: the standing bid is 0 and there is no leader. Every player starts active. There are up to 3 bidding steps.
   - In each step, every active player who is not the current leader chooses at the same time either to RAISE or to DROP.
   - A RAISE names a whole number at least the standing bid + 2. It may not be more than that player's current coins.
   - A player who DROPs is out of this round's auction.
   - A player with fewer coins than the standing bid + 2 must drop.
   - The leader is not asked and stays in.
4. Resolve each step:
   - If at least one player raised, the highest raise becomes the standing bid and its bidder becomes the leader.
   - Ties for the highest raise go to the tied player with the lowest score. If still tied, they go to the tied player whose seat comes first counting from seat ((r-1) mod n)+1 upward and wrapping around.
   - Players who raised but were outbid remain active.
   - Announce the standing bid, the leader, and who dropped.
   - If nobody raised in a step, bidding ends immediately. Bidding also ends after step 3.
5. Settle:
   - If there is a leader, the leader pays the standing bid from their coins. Their score changes by (their value - standing bid), which may be negative.
   - The leader's value for this round is announced. Nobody else's value is revealed.
   - If nobody ever raised, the item goes unsold and nothing changes.
6. Unspent coins carry over to the next round.

END: after round 8 the game ends.
variation.objective: The player with the highest score (total of value minus price over items won) wins. If scores are tied for the top, the tied player with more coins remaining wins. If still tied, the game is a draw among them.
variation.expected_effect: Bidding to value is no longer optimal. With 40 coins against 72 total value, players must pick their spots, save budget for their high cards and stop opponents from getting bargains. Because everyone's deck is identical and winners' values are revealed, players can count each opponent's remaining cards and track their coins, and use this to predict when a rival will push hard; jump bids and early drops become signals. Talk lets players propose bid rotation or claim to hold a low card. The players disagree because only one can win: a player who follows a 'you take this one' ring can be denied the reciprocal item later, or hand a rival a cheap high-value win, and so lose. 'Always pass' scores 0 and loses to anyone profiting. 'Always raise max' overpays into negative scores. Naive truthful bidding runs out of coins before its 14 and 16 cards appear.

balanced.evidence:
Every player holds the same eight values (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16; sum 72) and the same 40 coins, so no seat starts with more value or money. The seat tie-break rotates with the round, and the lowest-score tie-break favours whoever is behind, so no seat has a fixed edge from move order. The budget binds: 40 coins cannot buy items worth 72, so spending is a real planning decision.

Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule:
(a) Always DROP. Score is always 0. Any opponent who wins even one item at a price below its value (for example value 10 bought for 4, score +6) finishes ahead. Against random play, the random bidders sometimes overpay and go negative, but some opponent usually ends positive. This policy loses.
(b) Always raise the minimum (standing bid + 2) until leading. On a value-2 card it pays at least 2, scoring at most 0. When others push the price up it keeps raising, paying 4 to 6 or more for values of 2 to 6, which is negative. It also wastes coins needed for the 14 and 16 rounds. Against bidders who stop near their value, it trails. Not dominant.
(c) Always bid all coins in step 1. It pays 40 for one item, scoring at most 16 - 40 = -24. It loses to everyone, including always-drop.
(d) Always the highest legal raise each step. Same failure as (c).

No option is strictly better whatever others do. Whether to RAISE or DROP depends on your own value against the standing bid, your remaining coins, and your remaining high cards.

The 3-step cap creates a symmetric tension. The leader after step 2 cannot answer a step-3 raise. Non-leaders cannot wait, because their only alternative to raising is dropping. So players must decide how high to raise without becoming leader too early. This is a shared strategic trade-off, not a seat bias. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Rules cover every situation:
- Minimum raise is standing bid + 2, capped at current coins.
- A player who cannot afford the minimum is forced to drop.
- The leader is skipped; an outbid former leader stays active.
- Ties for the highest raise resolve by lowest score, then by rotating seat order.
- Bidding ends when nobody raises in a step, or after step 3.
- No raise at all means the item goes unsold.
- Settlement is arithmetic: pay the bid, score changes by value - bid, and negative scores are allowed.
- Coins carry over.
- The winner is decided by score, then coins, then a draw.

The game is finite: 8 rounds, at most 3 bidding steps each.

Limits check:
- steps_per_round 15 ≤ 20.
- choice_steps_per_round 4 (talk plus 3 bid steps) ≤ 4.
- attributes 11 ≤ 20; per-player coins and score are attribute types.
- hidden_elements 1 (private deck order) ≤ 3.
- random_draws_per_round 1: decks are shuffled once and each round deals the next card.
- rounds 8 ≤ 40.

Bids are simultaneous polls, as required. The game uses only supported features (private values, numeric bids, simultaneous choice, free-text talk) and needs no judge, board or clock.

Talk is simultaneous and sensible. Players compete for the same item, so they disagree. Messages give material to reason about, such as bluffing a high value to scare others off or claiming to have spent your 16. Following a proposal can cost you, for example dropping because someone claims a 16.

The end game does not collapse into a safe option. Leftover coins only break ties, so late rounds remain live bidding decisions.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance only sets the order in which each player's identical cards arrive. Everyone receives the same total value over the game, so the deal cannot hand anyone a better hand overall.

There is a lot to infer. Each player knows their own remaining cards. When a leader wins, their value is revealed, so others can strike that card from that opponent's possible remaining deck. Over rounds this narrows estimates of opponents' remaining high cards. Coins and scores are public, so opponents' budgets are known. Planning matters: save coins for your 14 and 16 rounds, and press when opponents are known to have spent their high cards or are short of coins.

When everyone plays well, a round's item tends to go to the holder of the highest value at a price set near the second-highest value or the budget cap. Over 8 rounds the timing luck partly evens out, because every player gets one 16, one 14, and so on. Outcomes are then decided by how well players read others, size their raises against the step-3 snipe, and manage coins. A bluffer or an overbidder is punished arithmetically.

Estimated chance share of the result: moderate, roughly 25-35%. The main chance element is high cards colliding in the same round. Good play can overcome it, for example by conceding a contested round cheaply and winning uncontested ones.
